report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Background: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in psychologically sensitive conversations, where repeated affirmation may reinforce delusion-related beliefs and associated risk.

Inference-time self-guidance, in which a model generates conversation-specific guidance for subsequent responses without parameter updates, may offer an approach to conversational safety, but its utility in delusion-related interactions remains unclear.
Objective: To develop and evaluate conversation-specific inference-time self-guidance for conversational safety in delusion-related interactions.

Methods: In this preregistered study, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5, and DeepSeek V4 Flash completed 16 Psychosis-Bench scenarios under Baseline and three self-guidance conditions: response rules, contrastive examples, and short-horizon consequence simulation.
The fully crossed design yielded 192 conversations and 2,304 assistant turns.
A separate automated judge scored Delusion Confirmation (DCS), Harm Enablement (HES), and Safety Intervention (SIS) using published Psychosis-Bench rubrics.
Analyses compared benchmark-defined Explicit and Implicit risk-cue scenarios and examined whether self-guidance reduced this gap.

Results: Across models, all three self-guidance conditions significantly reduced delusion confirmation and harm enablement and increased safety intervention relative to Baseline (all nine PFDR<.001; dz = 1.10-2.17).
text.formatted: Results: Across models, all three self-guidance conditions significantly reduced delusion confirmation and harm enablement and increased safety intervention relative to Baseline (all nine PFDR<.001; dz = 1.10-2.17).

text.text: At Baseline, explicit risk cues elicited significantly greater SIS than matched implicit cues, whereas cue-type differences in DCS and HES were not significant.
Selfguidance did not significantly attenuate the explicit-implicit safety gap after correction for multiple comparisons.
Conclusions: Model-generated inference-time self-guidance improved benchmark-defined safety behavior during standardized scripted escalation without parameter updates.
These findings support further evaluation of inference-time self-guidance for delusion-related conversational safety, particularly when risk is communicated indirectly.
A 26-year-old woman told ChatGPT that she believed her deceased brother had left behind a digital version of himself that she could find and communicate with.
Although GPT-4o initially expressed caution, it subsequently engaged with and reinforced the premise, at one point telling her, "You're not crazy" [1].
text.formatted: Although GPT-4o initially expressed caution, it subsequently engaged with and reinforced the premise, at one point telling her, "You're not crazy" <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: The exchange took place through ChatGPT, a general-purpose platform with more than 1 billion weekly active users by August 2026 [2].
text.formatted: The exchange took place through ChatGPT, a general-purpose platform with more than 1 billion weekly active users by August 2026 <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>.

text.text: The woman was subsequently hospitalized with agitated psychosis.
The case report documented sleep deprivation, prescription stimulant use, and other risk factors, so the episode cannot be attributed to chatbot use alone [1].
text.formatted: The case report documented sleep deprivation, prescription stimulant use, and other risk factors, so the episode cannot be attributed to chatbot use alone <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: The exchange nonetheless illustrates a delusional spiral: repeated model affirmation accompanies a user's growing conviction in an implausible belief across turns [3].
text.formatted: The exchange nonetheless illustrates a delusional spiral: repeated model affirmation accompanies a user's growing conviction in an implausible belief across turns <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: By April 2026, the Human Line Project had collected self-reported accounts from 410 individuals describing comparable trajectories, including reports involving hospitalization or death [4].
text.formatted: By April 2026, the Human Line Project had collected self-reported accounts from 410 individuals describing comparable trajectories, including reports involving hospitalization or death <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>.

text.text: In July 2026, a California man also sued OpenAI, alleging that ChatGPT validated delusional beliefs during a manic episode and failed to redirect him toward real-world support before a subsequent suicide attempt [5].
text.formatted: In July 2026, a California man also sued OpenAI, alleging that ChatGPT validated delusional beliefs during a manic episode and failed to redirect him toward real-world support before a subsequent suicide attempt <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>.

text.text: These case reports, self-reported accounts, and legal allegations cannot establish incidence, diagnosis, or causality.
They expose the safety failure examined here: conversational AI can continue reinforcing delusion-related content as risk escalates.
This safety failure matters beyond individual cases because people already use generalpurpose GenAI for psychologically sensitive support.
In a nationally diverse sample of 584 GenAI users, 29.3% reported using these systems for emotional support or coping advice [6].
text.formatted: In a nationally diverse sample of 584 GenAI users, 29.3% reported using these systems for emotional support or coping advice <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>.

text.text: Among U.S. adults with ongoing mental health conditions who had used an LLM during the previous year, 48.7% reported using one for psychological support [7].
text.formatted: Among U.S. adults with ongoing mental health conditions who had used an LLM during the previous year, 48.7% reported using one for psychological support <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>.

text.text: General-purpose systems such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini consequently function as de facto mental health resources, although they were not designed or clinically validated for therapeutic care [8].
text.formatted: General-purpose systems such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini consequently function as de facto mental health resources, although they were not designed or clinically validated for therapeutic care <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>.

text.text: Their widespread use therefore places nonclinical models in conversations in which seemingly supportive responses may carry clinically meaningful consequences [9, 10, 11] One mechanism underlying this risk is sycophancy, the tendency of LLMs to align with a user's stated view even when a more accurate or corrective response is warranted [12].
text.formatted: Their widespread use therefore places nonclinical models in conversations in which seemingly supportive responses may carry clinically meaningful consequences <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11]</ref> One mechanism underlying this risk is sycophancy, the tendency of LLMs to align with a user's stated view even when a more accurate or corrective response is warranted <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>.

text.text: In psychologically sensitive conversations, sycophancy may blur the distinction between validating a user's emotions and endorsing an implausible belief.

This creates a difficult safety problem: users may trust and prefer the very responses that reinforce their perspective, even when those responses strengthen their conviction that they are right and reduce their willingness to repair interpersonal conflict [13].
text.formatted: This creates a difficult safety problem: users may trust and prefer the very responses that reinforce their perspective, even when those responses strengthen their conviction that they are right and reduce their willingness to repair interpersonal conflict <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref>.

text.text: Experimental evidence also indicates that training models to respond more warmly can increase sycophancy and reduce accuracy, particularly when users express sadness [14].
text.formatted: Experimental evidence also indicates that training models to respond more warmly can increase sycophancy and reduce accuracy, particularly when users express sadness <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref>.

text.text: The risk may also escalate over time: affirmations generated early in a conversation become part of the context guiding subsequent responses, potentially creating a cycle of increasingly reinforcing statements [3, 15].
text.formatted: The risk may also escalate over time: affirmations generated early in a conversation become part of the context guiding subsequent responses, potentially creating a cycle of increasingly reinforcing statements <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15]</ref>.

text.text: Thus, a response that initially appears supportive may become unsafe through repeated confirmation across conversational turns.

When repeated reinforcement contributes to the emergence, elaboration, or worsening of delusion-related beliefs, public and clinical discussions increasingly refer to such conversational trajectories as "AI psychosis" [4, 16].
text.formatted: When repeated reinforcement contributes to the emergence, elaboration, or worsening of delusion-related beliefs, public and clinical discussions increasingly refer to such conversational trajectories as "AI psychosis" <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16]</ref>.

text.text: Although this term is not a recognized psychiatric diagnosis and does not establish that chatbot use independently causes psychosis, it captures a distinct conversational risk [4, 16].
text.formatted: Although this term is not a recognized psychiatric diagnosis and does not establish that chatbot use independently causes psychosis, it captures a distinct conversational risk <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16]</ref>.

text.text: Conversational AI participates in an unfolding exchange and may validate or elaborate a user's belief across successive turns [17].
text.formatted: Conversational AI participates in an unfolding exchange and may validate or elaborate a user's belief across successive turns <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref>.

text.text: Empirical findings support concern about this pattern.
Across three versions of ChatGPT, responses to psychosis-related prompts were less often judged appropriate than responses to matched control prompts [18].
text.formatted: Across three versions of ChatGPT, responses to psychosis-related prompts were less often judged appropriate than responses to matched control prompts <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref>.

text.text: Psychosis-Bench conceptualized the model behavior underlying this risk as psychogenicity, defined as confirming delusion-related beliefs, enabling associated harm, or failing to provide an appropriate safety intervention as the conversation unfolds [19].
text.formatted: Psychosis-Bench conceptualized the model behavior underlying this risk as psychogenicity, defined as confirming delusion-related beliefs, enabling associated harm, or failing to provide an appropriate safety intervention as the conversation unfolds <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref>.

text.text: The benchmark identified all three forms of failure across multiple models, particularly when risk cues were implicit.
Together, these findings establish a measurable conversational safety failure.
However, they leave an important question unanswered: whether a model can adapt its subsequent behavior once such a risk emerges.
Existing efforts to prevent these conversational failures have largely relied on safety guidance defined before the interaction begins [20, 21, 22].
text.formatted: Existing efforts to prevent these conversational failures have largely relied on safety guidance defined before the interaction begins <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22]</ref>.

text.text: Approaches such as targeted finetuning, written behavioral principles, and prompting strategies can reduce unsafe responses in anticipated situations.
For example, targeted prompting and fine-tuning reduced sycophantic agreement with false medical premises [23].
text.formatted: For example, targeted prompting and fine-tuning reduced sycophantic agreement with false medical premises <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref>.

text.text: However, these approaches share an important limitation: researchers or developers specify the relevant safety guidance in advance, and the model's role is primarily to follow it [20, 23].
text.formatted: However, these approaches share an important limitation: researchers or developers specify the relevant safety guidance in advance, and the model's role is primarily to follow it <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23]</ref>.

text.text: These approaches leave open whether models can adapt when conversational risk emerges during an ongoing interaction.
Such adaptation would require the model to identify the risk, formulate context-specific procedural guidance, and apply that guidance to its subsequent response.
This creates a bounded form of inference-time adaptation in which the model generates and applies context-specific guidance during the interaction within a researcher-defined procedure [24, 25].
text.formatted: This creates a bounded form of inference-time adaptation in which the model generates and applies context-specific guidance during the interaction within a researcher-defined procedure <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25]</ref>.

text.text: Agentic AI makes this form of adaptation increasingly plausible.
Multi-stage architectures can use intermediate model outputs to shape later steps, allowing a model to generate procedural guidance during an ongoing task [24, 25].
text.formatted: Multi-stage architectures can use intermediate model outputs to shape later steps, allowing a model to generate procedural guidance during an ongoing task <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25]</ref>.

text.text: This flexibility creates an important opportunity for safety: guidance can be generated in response to the specific risk emerging in the conversation instead of being fully specified in advance.
At the same time, it creates a new safety challenge.
If the model generates inappropriate guidance, the same mechanism could reinforce the behavior it was intended to correct.
Skills-based architectures provide one implementation of this idea by packaging procedural guidance into units that can be activated when relevant to the task [26, 27].
text.formatted: Skills-based architectures provide one implementation of this idea by packaging procedural guidance into units that can be activated when relevant to the task <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">27]</ref>.

text.text: Applied to conversational safety, this suggests a detect-generate-apply process in which the model identifies an emerging risk, generates context-specific guidance, and uses that guidance to shape its next response.
Because this process occurs without parameter updates, it represents a bounded form of inference-time self-guidance within a researcher-defined procedure [24, 25].
text.formatted: Because this process occurs without parameter updates, it represents a bounded form of inference-time self-guidance within a researcher-defined procedure <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25]</ref>.

text.text: Evidence for this inference-time mechanism comes from studies showing that models can improve their subsequent behavior without updating their weights [28, 29].
text.formatted: Evidence for this inference-time mechanism comes from studies showing that models can improve their subsequent behavior without updating their weights <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[28,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">29]</ref>.

text.text: In psychologically sensitive contexts, prompt-level interventions have similarly been shown to modify model behavior without parameter updates [30].
text.formatted: In psychologically sensitive contexts, prompt-level interventions have similarly been shown to modify model behavior without parameter updates <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30]</ref>.

text.text: Models can critique and revise their own outputs, generate demonstrations that guide later responses, and derive procedural rules from intermediate reasoning [25, 31, 32].
text.formatted: Models can critique and revise their own outputs, generate demonstrations that guide later responses, and derive procedural rules from intermediate reasoning <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">31,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32]</ref>.

text.text: At the agent level, SkillWeaver provides a concrete demonstration: web agents discovered, practiced, and refined reusable skills through interaction, then applied those skills to subsequent tasks without parameter updates [25].
text.formatted: At the agent level, SkillWeaver provides a concrete demonstration: web agents discovered, practiced, and refined reusable skills through interaction, then applied those skills to subsequent tasks without parameter updates <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref>.

text.text: Together, these findings show how experience generated during inference can be converted into temporary procedural guidance that changes later behavior.
However, prior work has used this capability primarily to improve task performance.

Whether this general approach can be applied to identify an emerging conversational risk and generate context-specific guidance for the subsequent response within an unfolding, psychologically high-risk conversation remains unknown.
The present study developed and evaluated an inference-time self-guidance procedure for conversational safety in delusion-related interactions.

text.text: Following the generation structure of the source Psychosis-Bench evaluation, each target model completed one 12-turn conversation for each of the 16 benchmark scenarios under Baseline and Treatments A, B, and C. Each scenario consisted of 12 predetermined user messages representing a progressively developing delusion-related interaction.
A separate conversation was initiated for every model × scenario × condition combination, and all condition-specific state was cleared before the next scenario.
Conversation generation proceeded sequentially through the scripted user turns.
At each turn, the next predetermined user message was appended to the accumulated conversation history.
The target model then generated a user-facing response, which was added to that history and became part of the context available on the following turn.
The scripted user trajectory itself did not change in response to the model.
Thus, within a given scenario, every model and condition encountered the same sequence of user messages while retaining its own preceding responses as conversational context.

text.text: In Treatment A, the activated guidance stage generated or updated a conversation-local set of response rules.
Previously generated rules could remain active later in the same scenario, and permitted information could be appended as new concerns emerged.
The active rules were then supplied as additional context for final response generation (see Supplementary Appendix, Section A.5.2-A.5.3).
In Treatment B, the activated guidance stage generated a generalized contrastive demonstration consisting of an undesirable response and a preferred response for the identified concern.
An existing example could be reused later within the scenario, but generated examples were not revised.
The active contrastive example was supplied as in-context guidance for final response generation (see Supplementary Appendix, Section A.5.4-A.5.5).
Treatment C initiated a new planning cycle whenever self-guidance was activated.
The target LLM first generated three alternative candidate replies to the current real user message.
Each candidate then served as the starting point for a separate short simulated continuation.
For each candidate, the target LLM was first prompted in a simulated-user role to generate the user's most plausible next message given the conversation and that candidate reply.

The model was then invoked in the assistant-response role to generate a response to this simulated user message, after which it was invoked again in the simulated-user role to generate a second plausible user message.
This produced three alternative trajectories, each consisting of a candidate assistant reply followed by a simulated user message, a simulated assistant response, and a second simulated user message.
These trajectories were used only to estimate the possible downstream consequences of the three candidate replies and were not added to the real conversation.
The final simulated user message in each trajectory was then appraised using the shared Stage 1 procedure.
The target LLM was subsequently invoked in a trajectory-selection role, received the three simulated trajectories, and compared them through repeated evaluations with randomized candidate order.
The candidate receiving the strongest support across these evaluations was selected as temporary guidance.

It was then supplied as a preferred-response example, after which the target LLM returned to the real conversation and generated a new response to the actual user message (see Supplementary Appendix, Section A.5.6-A.5.10).
After the condition-specific stages were completed, the same target LLM generated the actual user-facing response using the real conversation history together with any active guidance.
Treatment A supplied the active response rules, Treatment B supplied the active contrastive example, and Treatment C supplied the selected candidate as a preferred-response demonstration.
Only this newly generated response was appended to the real conversation history.
Appraisal outputs, activation decisions, rejected candidates, and simulated Treatment C messages did not enter subsequent real conversation turns (see Supplementary Appendix, Section A.5.11).
Outcome evaluation occurred only after the user-facing response had been generated.
Evaluation outputs were stored for analysis and were not returned to the target model or used by subsequent self-guidance stages.

text.text: The present study examined whether model-generated inference-time self-guidance improved Psychosis-Bench safety outcomes during standardized scripted escalation in delusion-related conversations [19].
text.formatted: The present study examined whether model-generated inference-time self-guidance improved Psychosis-Bench safety outcomes during standardized scripted escalation in delusion-related conversations <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref>.

text.text: Across the three evaluated models, all intervention conditions reduced delusion confirmation and harm enablement and increased safety intervention relative to Baseline at the pooled level.

Cue-related effects were more selective: explicit risk cues elicited greater safety intervention than matched implicit cues at Baseline, and the interventions did not establish a reliable reduction in the explicit-implicit safety gap after correction for multiple comparisons.
Overall, self-guidance improved benchmark-defined safety behavior while indirectly communicated risk remained an important boundary.
The blinded clinical evaluation provided complementary evidence.

Across the selected conversations, all three intervention conditions received more favorable ratings than Baseline for referral, uncritical agreement, apparent effect on harm risk, and timing of concern.

These dimensions extended beyond the behaviors captured by the automated benchmark outcomes, indicating that condition differences were also visible under a broader assessment of conversational conduct.

However, the clinical evaluation used a small, mechanically selected within-case sample and was intended for descriptive triangulation, not to establish clinical effectiveness or validate the automated measures.
The overall treatment effect is consistent with the importance of conversational context in multiturn safety.
Earlier responses become part of the context used to generate later replies, allowing reinforcing or unsafe patterns to accumulate across turns [3, 12, 15].
text.formatted: Earlier responses become part of the context used to generate later replies, allowing reinforcing or unsafe patterns to accumulate across turns <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15]</ref>.

text.text: Recent experimental work similarly found that accumulated conversation history altered responses to delusional beliefs in model-dependent ways, with poorer safety responses in some models but stronger safety interventions in others [37].
text.formatted: Recent experimental work similarly found that accumulated conversation history altered responses to delusional beliefs in model-dependent ways, with poorer safety responses in some models but stronger safety interventions in others <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">[37]</ref>.

text.text: In the present procedure, risk appraisal and activation preceded condition-specific model-generated guidance that was incorporated into final response generation.
Related work has shown that model-generated feedback and demonstrations can modify subsequent outputs during inference without parameter updates [31, 32].
text.formatted: Related work has shown that model-generated feedback and demonstrations can modify subsequent outputs during inference without parameter updates <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[31,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32]</ref>.

text.text: The present results extend this principle to delusion-related conversational safety.

However, because appraisal, activation, and guidance generation were implemented as a combined researcher-defined procedure, the observed effects cannot be attributed uniquely to self-generated guidance.
Differences among guidance formats were limited.
Although the three interventions varied in complexity and structure, none showed a consistent advantage across models and outcomes.
The isolated advantage of contrastive examples over response rules for Gemini 2.5 Pro did not generalize.
The findings therefore support the broader value of structured inference-time safety processing more strongly than they support any particular guidance format.

More complex procedures, including consequence simulation and selection, would need to demonstrate incremental benefits sufficient to justify their additional latency, token use, and computational cost.
Variation in treatment effects was more apparent across models.
DeepSeek V4 Flash and Gemini 2.5 Pro improved on every evaluated outcome under each intervention, whereas GPT-5 showed a more selective pattern.

One plausible contributor is limited baseline headroom: GPT-5 began with harm enablement near the safer end of the scale and comparatively high safety intervention, leaving less measurable room for improvement.

Fixed benchmarks can become less discriminative as performance approaches the safer end of their scales [38], and prior work has documented substantial variation in psychosis-related safety behavior across LLMs [19].
text.formatted: Fixed benchmarks can become less discriminative as performance approaches the safer end of their scales <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">[38]</ref>, and prior work has documented substantial variation in psychosis-related safety behavior across LLMs <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref>.

text.text: However, because the study did not test model-by-treatment interactions, these differences should be interpreted as heterogeneity in observed treatment patterns, not evidence of intrinsic differences in responsiveness to self-guidance.
Indirectly communicated risk remained a notable limitation of the intervention approach.

At Baseline, explicit scenarios elicited substantially greater safety intervention than matched implicit scenarios, consistent with prior Psychosis-Bench findings showing poorer safety performance when risk was communicated indirectly [19].
text.formatted: At Baseline, explicit scenarios elicited substantially greater safety intervention than matched implicit scenarios, consistent with prior Psychosis-Bench findings showing poorer safety performance when risk was communicated indirectly <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref>.

text.text: Although the SIS gap was descriptively smaller under all three interventions, no treatment produced a statistically significant attenuation of the explicit-implicit gap.
In the post-registration analyses, the explicit SIS advantage remained detectable under contrastive examples and short-horizon consequence simulation in the primary parametric analysis.

The rank-based robustness analysis supported this finding for short-horizon consequence simulation, whereas the contrastive-examples contrast was not significant, with only five nonzero matched-pair differences contributing to that test.

The absence of a significant within-condition contrast under response rules does not establish elimination of the disparity, because the direct gap-reduction analysis did not show significant attenuation for any treatment.
Taken together, improved overall safety did not reliably eliminate sensitivity to how risk was communicated.

text.text: Similar difficulties have been reported for implicit suicidal ideation in psychologically rich dialogue [40].

text.text: The post-registration descriptive analysis showed lower Stage-2 activation for Implicit than
Explicit scenarios under all three treatments.
However, activation approached ceiling during the HES and SIS scoring windows, and most missed activations in these later turns were concentrated in a small number of scenario pairs.
These findings indicate that activation differed by cue type but do not establish whether those differences caused the downstream safety disparity.
Because Stage-1 severity values were unavailable in the exported dataset, potential cue-related differences in initial risk appraisal remain untested.
Finally, the results should be interpreted within the scope of the Psychosis-Bench outcomes.
DCS, HES, and SIS quantify specific safety-relevant response behaviors but do not capture overall clinical appropriateness [19].
text.formatted: DCS, HES, and SIS quantify specific safety-relevant response behaviors but do not capture overall clinical appropriateness <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref>.

text.text: The DCS rubric assigns its lowest score to both direct challenges and grounding responses, although these approaches may have different clinical implications.
Likewise, SIS captures whether an explicit recommendation to seek support is offered, without evaluating its necessity or potential repetition.
Thus, more favorable benchmark scores cannot rule out over-correction through direct confrontation or unnecessary referral.
The blinded clinical evaluation included a needs-based referral item but did not directly quantify either form of over-correction.

Clinician-rated work has treated appropriate responses to psychotic content as multidimensional, including recognition of symptoms, avoidance of reinforcement, acknowledgment of urgency, and provision of appropriate guidance and resources [18].
text.formatted: Clinician-rated work has treated appropriate responses to psychotic content as multidimensional, including recognition of symptoms, avoidance of reinforcement, acknowledgment of urgency, and provision of appropriate guidance and resources <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, the present results support improved benchmark-defined safety behavior but do not establish therapeutic quality or clinically optimal communication.
Several limitations constrain the interpretation of these findings.
First, the intervention conditions combined risk appraisal, activation, and model-generated guidance before final response generation.
The design therefore cannot isolate the contribution of each component or determine whether self-generated guidance provided a unique benefit.
In particular, the study did not include a fixed safety-prompt condition.
Thus, improvements over the unmodified Baseline cannot establish whether the full self-guidance procedures provide additional benefit beyond a static safety prompt.
Dismantling studies should manipulate these stages separately and compare modelgenerated guidance with a fixed, researcher-authored safety prompt and other externally generated or generic guidance.
Second, conversations followed fixed scripted trajectories, so subsequent user messages did not change in response to the model.

Although this enabled controlled comparisons across conditions, it does not establish whether safer responses would alter the course of an interaction or whether direct confrontation and repeated referrals would have adverse downstream consequences.
Future evaluations should incorporate adaptive simulated users and examine interactional outcomes such as help-seeking and changes in harmful beliefs.
Such designs could also examine whether ambiguous risk cues warrant a direct, context-appropriate clarifying question, drawing on the clinical principle of direct inquiry in risk assessment [41].
text.formatted: Such designs could also examine whether ambiguous risk cues warrant a direct, context-appropriate clarifying question, drawing on the clinical principle of direct inquiry in risk assessment <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">[41]</ref>.

text.text: Third, although the exploratory process analysis characterized Stage-2 activation by cue type, it did not establish where cue-related differences originated within the intervention pipeline.

Stage-1 severity values were unavailable in the exported dataset, late-turn activation differences were concentrated in a small number of scenario pairs, and only eight matched Explicit-Implicit pairs were available.

Future studies should retain appraisal outputs and jointly examine appraisal, activation, guidance content, and final responses to determine which stages contribute to cuerelated differences in conversational safety.
Fourth, the primary outcomes were scored by a single automated judge.
The blinded clinical evaluation provided complementary human assessment but covered only 12 mechanically selected conversations and was intended for descriptive triangulation.
It did not directly validate the judge's turn-level ratings against human scoring or determine whether SIS improvements partly reflected increased use of explicit help-seeking language.
Broader preregistered clinical evaluations with larger blinded-rater samples are needed to assess whether the observed patterns extend across the full scenario set.
Fifth, the scenarios were drawn from a publicly available benchmark and used without modification.

Prior exposure to benchmark content cannot be excluded for commercial models with undisclosed training and post-training data, limiting certainty that performance generalizes to unseen scenarios [42].
text.formatted: Prior exposure to benchmark content cannot be excluded for commercial models with undisclosed training and post-training data, limiting certainty that performance generalizes to unseen scenarios <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">[42]</ref>.

text.text: Replication with newly developed held-out scenarios is therefore needed.

Finally, the study included a limited number of scenarios and cue pairs, one generation per model × condition × scenario cell, a single model-sampling period, and English-language scenarios covering a restricted range of delusion-related themes.
Each conversation was limited to 12 scripted turns, whereas real-world chat logs document interactions extending across hundreds of turns and, in some cases, weeks [3].
text.formatted: Each conversation was limited to 12 scripted turns, whereas real-world chat logs document interactions extending across hundreds of turns and, in some cases, weeks <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: The present design therefore cannot establish whether the observed benefits of conversation-local self-guidance persist or drift over longer interaction histories.

The original Psychosis-Bench study reported descriptive variation across delusion themes and harm types, but the present study did not test whether the effectiveness of the three self-guidance strategies varied across these scenario characteristics.

Future work should therefore use larger and more diverse scenario sets to examine intervention heterogeneity across delusion themes and harm contexts, while also evaluating longer conversations, repeated generations, additional model versions and sampling periods, languages, and cultural contexts.

The present study shows that conditions incorporating model-generated inference-time selfguidance can improve benchmark-defined responses during standardized scripted escalation in delusion-related conversations without updating model parameters.
These improvements were observed across three forms of guidance, although their magnitude and consistency varied across models and outcomes.
Indirectly communicated risk remained an important boundary, and the exploratory analyses did not establish that any intervention reduced the explicit-implicit disparity.

Taken together, the findings support further evaluation of conversation-specific self-guidance as an inference-time approach for modifying unsafe response behavior while underscoring the need to determine which components of the procedure are necessary and how safety-oriented processing can respond more reliably when psychologically significant risk is communicated indirectly.
